### Quick answer Yes, if the data you’re deleting is truly no longer needed, removing it will free up space and keep you under Supabase’s free‑plan limit. Just be sure you have a backup (or confirm you’re ready to lose it) and that you only delete rows that belong to you. --- ## Why this is safe 👍 | What you’re doing | Risk | Confidence | Notes | |-------------------|------|------------|-------| | Deleting rows you’re sure are useless | ❌ | 10/10 | ✔️ Supabase allows you to run `DELETE` statements safely. | | Making a backup first | ✔️ | 10/10 | If you want a safety net, take a snapshot before you delete. | | Running the delete on only your table & user data | ✔️ | 10/10 | Supabase limits you to the tables you own, so no accidental cross‑table damage. | --- ## Step‑by‑step plan (no code knowledge needed) | Step | Action | How to do it | |------|--------|--------------| | **1. Log into Supabase** | Open `https://app.supabase.com` and select your project. | Click the **Project** you’re on (the one showing the “Database” tab). | | **2. View current usage** | Check how close you are to the free‑plan limit. | In the sidebar, click **Analytics → Storage**. The banner will say “You’re at X% of the 10‑GB limit.” | | **3. Identify old data** | Pick a table or records that are obsolete. | • Think of tables you’ve added yearly (e.g. `logs`, `temp_data`).
• In **Database → Table editor**, click the table name. | | **4. Take a backup (recommended)** | Export the entire table or a snapshot. | 1. In Table editor, click the three dots ↙ next to the table name.
2. Choose **Export CSV** or **Download Table**. | | **5. Delete the unwanted rows** | Run a simple delete query. | 1. Go to **SQL editor** (sidebar → SQL).
2. Type a query like:
```sql\nDELETE FROM my_old_table WHERE created_at < '2023-01-01';\n```\n—replace `my_old_table` and the date with your own condition.
3. Click **RUN**. | | **6. Verify space freed** | Check the storage bar again. | Look at the **Storage** analytics after the run; you should see a drop in usage. | | **7. Confirm everything is still fine** | Test a page or API that reads from the table. | Open the part of your app that pulls from that table—data should still show for current rows. | --- ## Things to double‑check 1. **Confirm the data is not needed** – ask yourself: “Will I or any user ever need this row again?” 2. **Only delete from tables you own** – Supabase won’t let you touch tables of other projects, so you’re safe. 3. **Keep a backup** – Even if you think it’s safe, having a CSV backup lets you restore if something’s missing. 4. **Re‑run the storage graph** – After the delete you should see the bar move lower. If it stays the same, double‑check the query or try deleting in smaller batches. --- ## Quick “What‑if” scenarios | Scenario | What to do | |----------|-----------| | I see the usage bar still high after deleting | Maybe I didn’t delete enough rows or I deleted the wrong table. Reload the SQL editor and run the query again with a broader `WHERE` clause (e.g., `id < 1000`). | | Something else is using space (files, RLS logs) | Check **Storage → Objects** and **Database → Logs** to see if files or logs are bloating. Supabase occasionally keeps large log files; you can delete old ones there. | | I’m unsure about the data | Export the whole table as CSV and keep it in a safe folder on your computer before deletion. | --- ### Final checklist - [ ] I know which rows are “old” and can be removed. - [ ] I have exported (or saved) a copy of those rows. - [ ] I ran a precise `DELETE` query in the Supabase SQL editor. - [ ] The usage bar shows a meaningful drop. - [ ] A quick test still shows current data works. If you tick all the boxes, you’ve safely freed space without risking the rest of your app! If you hit any hiccups while following the steps, let me know, and we can troubleshoot together.
